description: American settlements — from Spanish missions and French trading posts to Puritan towns, boomtowns, and ghost towns — take root and stay on the map from their founding year onward, growing (or vanishing) as reflected in census counts and, where a place was abandoned, its end date.

events.title: Fort Caroline founded
events.desc: French Huguenot colonists built this fort near the mouth of the St. Johns River in Florida, France's first colonial foothold in North America. Spanish forces from the newly founded St. Augustine attacked and destroyed the fort, killing most of the colonists and ending France's claim to Florida.

events.title: Popham Colony founded
events.desc: English colonists built Fort St. George at the mouth of the Kennebec River the same year as Jamestown, an early rival attempt at permanent settlement. A brutal winter, the death of colony leader George Popham, and dwindling supplies led the surviving colonists to abandon the fort and sail home after little more than a year.

events.title: Taos founded
events.desc: Spanish colonists settled near the centuries-old Taos Pueblo, forming one of the earliest European communities in the Southwest.

events.title: Wessagusset Colony founded
events.desc: A short-lived trading colony on Massachusetts Bay, founded by London merchants; poor planning and conflict with the Pilgrims led to its collapse within a year. The colony fell apart amid starvation and conflict; survivors scattered or joined Plymouth Colony.

events.title: Dover founded
events.desc: A fishing and trading outpost on the Cocheco River, generally considered the oldest permanent European settlement in New Hampshire.

events.title: Albany (Fort Orange) founded
events.desc: Dutch fur traders built Fort Orange on the upper Hudson River; it grew into Albany, one of the oldest continuously chartered cities in the original colonies.

events.title: New York City founded
events.desc: Dutch colonists established a fur-trading settlement at the tip of Manhattan Island; it would be renamed New York after the English took control in 1664.

events.title: Salem founded
events.desc: Founded by English fishermen and Puritan settlers, Salem later became infamous for the 1692 witch trials.

events.title: Charlestown founded
events.desc: Settled just before Boston across the harbor, Charlestown was later annexed by its larger neighbor.

events.title: Lynn founded
events.desc: An early Massachusetts Bay Colony settlement that became a center of shoemaking.

events.title: Boston founded
events.desc: Puritan colonists settled the Shawmut Peninsula, founding what became the political and commercial center of New England.

events.title: Cambridge founded
events.desc: Founded as "Newtowne," it was renamed Cambridge and became home to Harvard College in 1636.

events.title: Dorchester founded
events.desc: One of the original Massachusetts Bay Colony towns, later absorbed into the city of Boston.

events.title: Portsmouth founded
events.desc: Settled as Strawbery Banke, a fishing and trading post that grew into New Hampshire's colonial capital.

events.title: Roxbury founded
events.desc: Founded alongside Boston, Roxbury remained a separate town for over two centuries before annexation.

events.title: Watertown founded
events.desc: Founded by Puritan settlers on the Charles River as part of the Massachusetts Bay Colony's first wave of towns.

events.title: York founded
events.desc: Generally considered the oldest incorporated town in Maine.

events.title: Ipswich founded
events.desc: An early Massachusetts Bay Colony town known for its shipbuilding and lace-making traditions.

events.title: St. Mary's City founded
events.desc: Founded by English Catholic settlers, St. Mary's City served as Maryland's first colonial capital. The colony's capital moved to Annapolis, and St. Mary's City rapidly declined into little more than farmland; it is now preserved as an archaeological site.

events.title: Wethersfield founded
events.desc: One of the three original Connecticut River towns, predating the colony of Connecticut itself.

events.title: Concord founded
events.desc: The first inland town in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, later the site of the war's opening battle in 1775.

events.title: Hartford founded
events.desc: Founded by Puritan settlers under Thomas Hooker, Hartford became the capital of the Connecticut Colony.

events.title: Old Saybrook founded
events.desc: Founded at the mouth of the Connecticut River as the seat of the short-lived Saybrook Colony.

events.title: Providence founded
events.desc: Founded by Roger Williams after his banishment from Massachusetts Bay for advocating religious tolerance.

events.title: Saco founded
events.desc: An early fishing and lumber settlement on the Maine coast.

events.title: Springfield founded
events.desc: Founded on the Connecticut River, Springfield remained part of Massachusetts rather than joining Connecticut.

events.title: Exeter founded
events.desc: Founded by Reverend John Wheelwright after his own banishment from Massachusetts Bay.

events.title: New Haven founded
events.desc: Founded by Puritan merchants as the center of the separate New Haven Colony, later absorbed into Connecticut.

events.title: Portsmouth (Rhode Island) founded
events.desc: Founded by Anne Hutchinson and other religious dissenters exiled from Massachusetts Bay.

events.title: Guilford founded
events.desc: A Puritan farming town founded along the Connecticut shoreline.

events.title: Newport founded
events.desc: Founded on Aquidneck Island, Newport grew into a major colonial seaport and center of religious tolerance.

events.title: Warwick founded
events.desc: Founded by Samuel Gorton, another dissenter who fell out with the Massachusetts Bay authorities.

events.title: Annapolis founded
events.desc: Founded by Puritan settlers as Providence, it was renamed Annapolis in 1694 when it became Maryland's new capital.

events.title: New Castle founded
events.desc: Founded by the Dutch as New Amstel on the Delaware River, later taken by the English and renamed.

events.title: Schenectady founded
events.desc: Founded by Dutch colonists on the Mohawk River as a farming and trading settlement west of Albany.

events.title: Newark founded
events.desc: Founded by Puritan settlers from Connecticut on the banks of the Passaic River.

events.title: Charleston founded
events.desc: English colonists established Charles Town, which grew into the wealthiest and most cosmopolitan city in the colonial South.

events.title: Prairie du Chien founded
events.desc: A French fur-trading post at the confluence of the Wisconsin and Mississippi Rivers, among the oldest European settlements in the upper Midwest.

events.title: Burlington founded
events.desc: Founded by English Quakers, Burlington briefly served as capital of West Jersey.

events.title: Philadelphia founded
events.desc: William Penn laid out the city on land granted by the English crown, planning it on a grid as a haven for religious dissenters.

events.title: Ysleta (El Paso) founded
events.desc: Spanish refugees from the Pueblo Revolt founded this mission settlement, considered the oldest continuous European settlement in Texas.

events.title: Germantown founded
events.desc: Founded by German and Dutch Quaker and Mennonite immigrants, it became one of the first German settlements in America.

events.title: Perth Amboy founded
events.desc: Founded as the capital of the colony of East Jersey at a strategic point on Raritan Bay.

events.title: Pensacola founded
events.desc: Spain established a presidio on the Gulf Coast to guard against French expansion, making it one of the oldest European settlements in the continental United States.

events.title: Biloxi founded
events.desc: Founded by French colonists, Biloxi served as the first capital of French Louisiana.

events.title: Cahokia founded
events.desc: Founded by French missionaries across the Mississippi from present-day St. Louis, Cahokia is considered the oldest permanent European settlement in Illinois.

events.title: Detroit (Fort Pontchartrain) founded
events.desc: Founded by French officer Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac as a fort controlling the strait between Lakes Erie and Huron.

events.title: Mobile founded
events.desc: Founded by French colonists as the first capital of French Louisiana before the seat moved to Biloxi and later New Orleans.

events.title: Kaskaskia founded
events.desc: A French mission and trading town that later served as the first capital of the Illinois Territory and then the state of Illinois. Catastrophic Mississippi River flooding shifted the river's channel and destroyed most of the town, leaving only a tiny remnant on an island cut off from the Illinois mainland.

events.title: Bath founded
events.desc: North Carolina's oldest incorporated town, founded as a port on the Pamlico River.

events.title: Albuquerque founded
events.desc: Founded by Spanish colonists and named for a Spanish duke, Albuquerque grew along the Rio Grande as a farming and trading town.

events.title: New Bern founded
events.desc: Founded by Swiss and German Palatine settlers and named for the Swiss city of Bern.

events.title: Beaufort (South Carolina) founded
events.desc: Founded as a port town on the South Carolina Lowcountry coast, later prospering from indigo and rice.

events.title: Edenton founded
events.desc: An early North Carolina port town that briefly served as the colony's capital.

events.title: Nacogdoches founded
events.desc: Founded around a Spanish mission among the Caddo people in East Texas.

events.title: Natchez (Fort Rosalie) founded
events.desc: French colonists built Fort Rosalie above the Mississippi River on land belonging to the Natchez people.

events.title: Green Bay (La Baye) founded
events.desc: Built around an earlier French mission and trading post, Green Bay is considered Wisconsin's oldest settlement.

events.title: New Orleans founded
events.desc: French colonists established the port city near the mouth of the Mississippi, which passed to Spanish and then back to French control before the 1803 Louisiana Purchase.

events.title: San Antonio founded
events.desc: Spanish colonists established a mission and presidio along the San Antonio River; the settlement grew into the largest town in Spanish and later Mexican Texas.

events.title: Trenton founded
events.desc: Founded by Quaker settlers at the falls of the Delaware River, later the site of Washington's pivotal 1776 crossing.

events.title: Baltimore founded
events.desc: The town was chartered on the Patapsco River as a tobacco-shipping port for the Maryland colony.

events.title: Georgetown (South Carolina) founded
events.desc: Founded at the mouth of the Pee Dee and Waccamaw Rivers, it grew into a major rice-exporting port.

events.title: Vincennes founded
events.desc: Founded as a French fur-trading post on the Wabash River, later the site of a decisive Revolutionary War campaign.

events.title: Savannah founded
events.desc: Founded by James Oglethorpe as the first settlement in the colony of Georgia, laid out on a distinctive grid of public squares.

events.title: Ste. Genevieve founded
events.desc: Founded by French colonists, it is considered the oldest permanent European settlement in present-day Missouri.

events.title: Wilmington (North Carolina) founded
events.desc: Founded on the Cape Fear River, Wilmington grew into North Carolina's leading colonial port.

events.title: Goliad founded
events.desc: Founded as a Spanish mission and presidio in South Texas, later the site of a notorious massacre during the Texas Revolution.

events.title: Laredo founded
events.desc: Founded by Spanish colonists on the north bank of the Rio Grande as a ranching settlement.

events.title: St. Louis founded
events.desc: French fur traders established a trading post on the Mississippi, which later became a key jumping-off point for westward expeditions and migration.

events.title: Mission San Diego de Alcalá founded
events.desc: Founded by Father Junípero Serra, this was the first of the 21 Spanish missions in Alta California, the seed of present-day San Diego.

events.title: Mission San Carlos Borromeo (Carmel) founded
events.desc: Serra's second mission became his headquarters and burial place, and grew into present-day Carmel-by-the-Sea.

events.title: Mission San Antonio de Padua founded
events.desc: Established in a remote inland valley, this mission became a center of irrigation farming and craft production.

events.title: Mission San Gabriel Arcángel founded
events.desc: One of the most productive missions, its farmland and orchards helped supply the settlement that became Los Angeles.

events.title: Mission San Luis Obispo de Tolosa founded
events.desc: Founded partway along the mission chain, it gave its name to the city that grew around it.

events.title: Mission San Francisco de Asís (Dolores) founded
events.desc: Founded the same year as American independence, this mission became the nucleus of San Francisco.

events.title: Mission San Juan Capistrano founded
events.desc: Known for its swallows and its Great Stone Church, later damaged by an 1812 earthquake.

events.title: San Francisco founded
events.desc: Spain established a fort and mission on the San Francisco Bay, the seed of a small settlement that stayed modest for seven decades.

events.title: Mission Santa Clara de Asís founded
events.desc: Repeatedly relocated due to flooding, it eventually became the site of Santa Clara University.

events.title: Los Angeles founded
events.desc: Spanish colonial authorities established a small farming pueblo, decades before it became part of Mexico and, later, the United States.

events.title: Mission San Buenaventura founded
events.desc: The last mission founded by Junípero Serra himself, on the coast that became Ventura.

events.title: Mission Santa Barbara founded
events.desc: Became an important center of Franciscan activity and gave its name to the city and channel.

events.title: Mission La Purísima Concepción founded
events.desc: One of the most heavily restored missions today, near present-day Lompoc.

events.title: Cincinnati founded
events.desc: Settlers established a town on the Ohio River that grew rapidly as a meatpacking and manufacturing center, earning the nickname "Porkopolis."

events.title: Baltimore: population 16,359
events.desc: Baltimore was already among the five largest cities in the new republic.

events.title: Boston: population 18,320
events.desc: Boston ranked as the fourth-largest city in the young United States.

events.title: Charleston: population 13,503
events.desc: Charleston ranked among the five largest cities in the country, built on rice, indigo, and the trade in enslaved people; its relative rank fell over the next century as inland and western cities outgrew it.

events.title: New York City: population 33,131
events.desc: The first US census recorded New York as the country's largest city, a rank it has held in every census since.

events.title: Philadelphia: population 28,522
events.desc: Philadelphia was the new nation's second-largest city and, for a time, its capital.

events.title: Mission Nuestra Señora de la Soledad founded
events.desc: A remote and often struggling mission in the Salinas Valley.

events.title: Mission Santa Cruz founded
events.desc: Founded across the San Lorenzo River from a Spanish pueblo, forming the twin settlements that became Santa Cruz.

events.title: Mission San Fernando Rey de España founded
events.desc: Founded in the San Fernando Valley, now part of Los Angeles.

events.title: Mission San José founded
events.desc: Once one of the most prosperous missions, its lands later became part of Fremont, California.

events.title: Mission San Juan Bautista founded
events.desc: Built beside the San Andreas Fault, its large church still overlooks the original town plaza.

events.title: Mission San Miguel Arcángel founded
events.desc: Known for its well-preserved original interior murals and decoration.

events.title: Mission San Luis Rey de Francia founded
events.desc: The largest and most prosperous of the missions, earning it the nickname "King of the Missions."

events.title: Mission Santa Inés founded
events.desc: Founded to ease crowding at neighboring missions, near present-day Solvang.

events.title: New Orleans: population 17,000
events.desc: Now under US control, New Orleans was already a major port for cotton and sugar shipped down the Mississippi.

events.title: St. Louis: population 1,400
events.desc: St. Louis remained a small frontier river town in the years just after the Louisiana Purchase.

events.title: Mission San Rafael Arcángel founded
events.desc: Originally built as a hospital outpost for ailing mission residents, north of San Francisco Bay.

events.title: Cahawba founded
events.desc: Founded at the confluence of the Cahaba and Alabama Rivers, Cahawba served as Alabama's first state capital. The capital moved to Tuscaloosa in 1826, and repeated flooding and the loss of its county seat status in 1866 led to the town's gradual abandonment by the turn of the century.

events.title: Mission San Francisco Solano founded
events.desc: The last and northernmost of the California missions, founded at Sonoma under Mexican rule.

events.title: New York City: population 202,589
events.desc: New York passed the 200,000 mark, its growth fueled by the newly opened Erie Canal, which routed western trade through the port.

events.title: Chicago founded
events.desc: The settlement at the mouth of the Chicago River, with only a few hundred residents, was formally incorporated as a town; it became a city just four years later.

events.title: Houston founded
events.desc: Brothers Augustus and John Allen founded the town on Buffalo Bayou and named it for Sam Houston shortly after his victory at San Jacinto; it briefly served as capital of the Republic of Texas.

events.title: Austin founded
events.desc: The Republic of Texas relocated its capital to a small settlement then known as Waterloo, renaming it for empresario Stephen F. Austin.

events.title: San Francisco: population 900
events.desc: Just before gold was discovered nearby, the renamed town of San Francisco was still a sleepy port of a few hundred people.

events.title: Austin: population 629
events.desc: As the seat of Texas's government, Austin remained a small frontier town on the edge of settled territory.

events.title: Baltimore: population 169,054
events.desc: Rail and shipping trade made Baltimore the country's second-largest city for a time in the mid-1800s.

events.title: Boston: population 136,881
events.desc: Landfill projects steadily expanded the peninsula's buildable area as the population grew.

events.title: Chicago: population 29,963
events.desc: Rail lines converging on Chicago were turning it into the Midwest's dominant transportation hub.

events.title: Cincinnati: population 115,435
events.desc: Cincinnati had become one of the largest cities in the country, rivaling the older cities of the East Coast.

events.title: Houston: population 2,396
events.desc: Houston remained a modest bayou town, still well behind San Antonio and the port of Galveston in size.

events.title: Los Angeles: population 1,610
events.desc: At the time of California statehood, Los Angeles was still a small, dusty ranching town, far smaller than San Francisco to the north.

events.title: New Orleans: population 116,375
events.desc: New Orleans ranked among the five largest US cities, its port among the busiest in the country.

events.title: New York City: population 515,547
events.desc: The city more than doubled in two decades as immigration surged, especially from Ireland and Germany.

events.title: Philadelphia: population 121,376
events.desc: Manufacturing and shipbuilding drove steady growth through the first half of the century.

events.title: San Antonio: population 3,488
events.desc: San Antonio was already Texas's largest town, its economy built on ranching and a population mixing Tejano, German, and Anglo settlers.

events.title: San Francisco: population 34,776
events.desc: The Gold Rush transformed the town almost overnight into a booming, chaotic city of prospectors, merchants, and speculators.

events.title: St. Louis: population 77,860
events.desc: Steamboat trade on the Mississippi and Missouri Rivers fueled explosive growth in just a few decades.

events.title: Bodie founded
events.desc: A gold-mining camp in the California high desert that boomed to roughly 10,000 residents at its 1870s peak. Dwindling ore, harsh winters, and the diversion of resources to World War II led to the closure of the last mine and the town's abandonment; it is now preserved in a state of "arrested decay."

events.title: Grafton founded
events.desc: Mormon pioneers founded this farming settlement on the Virgin River in southern Utah. Repeated flooding, isolation, and the difficulty of farming the land led the last residents to leave by the mid-1940s.

events.title: Virginia City founded
events.desc: Founded on Nevada's Comstock Lode, one of the richest silver strikes in American history, drawing tens of thousands of prospectors.

events.title: Austin: population 3,494
events.desc: Austin's population grew more than fivefold in a decade as the state government and surrounding ranching economy expanded.

events.title: San Antonio: population 8,235
events.desc: Heavy German immigration helped San Antonio become the largest town in Texas, ahead of the Gulf port of Galveston.

events.title: Bannack founded
events.desc: A gold-rush boomtown that briefly served as Montana's first territorial capital. Remote location and exhausted gold deposits led to a long, slow decline; the last residents left around 1970, and Bannack is now a preserved state park.

events.title: Centralia (Pennsylvania) founded
events.desc: A Pennsylvania coal town built above rich anthracite deposits. An underground mine fire, accidentally ignited in 1962, spread beneath the town and made it uninhabitable; most residents were relocated and the borough was effectively abandoned, though the fire still burns today.

events.title: South Pass City founded
events.desc: A Wyoming gold-rush town that briefly boomed to several thousand residents and hosted an early vote for women's suffrage in the territory. The gold played out quickly, and the town's population dwindled to nearly nothing by mid-century; it is now a preserved historic site.

events.title: Chicago: population 298,977
events.desc: Chicago's population had grown roughly tenfold in twenty years, driven by railroads, stockyards, and manufacturing.

events.title: Deadwood founded
events.desc: A lawless Black Hills gold-rush camp that grew rapidly after gold was discovered on nearby Deadwood Gulch.

events.title: Tombstone founded
events.desc: A silver-mining boomtown in the Arizona desert, later famous for the 1881 gunfight near the O.K. Corral.

events.title: New York City: population 1,206,299
events.desc: New York became the first US city recorded with over a million residents.

events.title: San Antonio: population 20,550
events.desc: The arrival of the Galveston, Harrisburg and San Antonio Railway in 1877 opened a new era of growth for the city.

events.title: Calico founded
events.desc: A silver-mining camp in the Mojave Desert that grew to support around 500 mines at its peak. A collapse in silver prices in the 1890s emptied the town within about fifteen years of its founding.

events.title: Austin: population 22,258
events.desc: Austin had grown into a modest state capital, still far smaller than Texas's commercial hubs of San Antonio, Houston, and Galveston.

events.title: Baltimore: population 508,957
events.desc: Baltimore had grown into a major manufacturing and port city on the East Coast.

events.title: Boston: population 560,892
events.desc: Boston had grown into a major industrial and financial center, though it slipped in national rank as western cities boomed.

events.title: Chicago: population 1,698,575
events.desc: Rebuilt after the Great Fire of 1871, Chicago had become the country's second-largest city.

events.title: Cincinnati: population 325,902
events.desc: Growth continued but at a slower pace as rail hubs further west, like Chicago, drew trade away.

events.title: Houston: population 44,633
events.desc: Railroads converging on Houston were turning it into a major commercial center, just before the nearby Spindletop oil discovery transformed the regional economy.

events.title: Los Angeles: population 102,479
events.desc: Rail connections and land promotion sparked rapid growth in the late 1800s, setting up the city's explosive twentieth-century expansion.

events.title: New Orleans: population 287,104
events.desc: Growth slowed relative to northern and midwestern rivals, though the port remained economically vital.

events.title: New York City: population 3,437,202
events.desc: The 1898 consolidation with Brooklyn and other boroughs into Greater New York nearly tripled the city's official population overnight.

events.title: Philadelphia: population 1,293,697
events.desc: Philadelphia remained the country's third-largest city, behind only New York and Chicago.

events.title: San Antonio: population 53,321
events.desc: San Antonio was Texas's largest city, its cattle-trail and railroad connections drawing steady growth.

events.title: San Francisco: population 342,782
events.desc: San Francisco had become the largest and most important city on the West Coast.

events.title: St. Louis: population 575,238
events.desc: St. Louis had grown into the fourth-largest city in the country ahead of hosting the 1904 World's Fair.

events.title: Kennecott founded
events.desc: A remote Alaskan copper-mining town built around one of the richest copper deposits ever found. The mine was depleted and the company shut down operations, and the town was abandoned almost overnight.

events.title: Rhyolite founded
events.desc: A Nevada gold-rush town that grew from tents to a modern city of several thousand in just a few years. The gold deposits played out almost as quickly as they were found, and the town was essentially deserted within about fifteen years.
